01.actor: Shmuel's father and Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
01.event: A bill of divorce signed by one Androlinai of Neharde'a was found, and Shmuel's father sent the question of its validity to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia.
01.turn: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, rather than accepting it, replied that all of Neharde'a must be searched for another man of that name.
01.outcome: The instruction to search is given; the result of the search is not told.
01.summary: A bill of divorce turned up in Neharde'a, signed by a man named Androlinai, and it was unclear whether it was really from the woman's husband. Shmuel's father sent the question to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia in the Land of Israel. He wrote back that the whole city must be checked for another man with the same name.
01.missing: What the search found and whether the woman was permitted to remarry.

02.event: Ameimar permitted Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mehoza.
02.turn: Rav Ashi challenged him, pointing out that three academies did not teach the lenient tradition he seemed to rely on.
02.outcome: Ameimar did not accept the objection, because he had heard the ruling directly from Rav Zevid of Neharde'a.
02.summary: Ameimar allowed Rav Huna bar Natan to marry a woman from Mehoza, a town of doubtful lineage. Rav Ashi questioned him, noting that the schools of Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa and Rav Zevid did not teach the tradition that would allow it. Ameimar held his ground, because he had heard the ruling in person from Rav Zevid of Neharde'a.

03.event: Ulla praised Rav Hamnuna's learning but lamented that he came from Harpanya, a town of flawed lineage.
03.turn: Rav Hamnuna was ashamed, and Ulla asked him where he paid his poll tax.
03.outcome: When he answered Pum Nahara, Ulla declared that he was therefore from Pum Nahara and his lineage was sound.
03.summary: Rav Hamnuna was studying before Ulla, who exclaimed what a great man he was, if only he were not from Harpanya, a town known for flawed lineage. Rav Hamnuna was humiliated. Ulla then asked where he paid his poll tax, and when he said Pum Nahara, Ulla concluded that he belonged to Pum Nahara and his lineage was not in question.

04.event: Judges ruled a case following Rabbi Tarfon, and Reish Lakish overturned their decision.
04.turn: Rabbi Yohanan criticized him for treating the error as if it were a matter of Torah law.
04.outcome: The rebuke is given; whether the reversal stood is not said.
04.summary: Some judges decided an inheritance case following Rabbi Tarfon's view, and Reish Lakish reversed their ruling and returned the money. Rabbi Yohanan rebuked him, saying he had acted as though the judges had erred in Torah law, where a mistaken ruling must be undone.
04.missing: How the matter was resolved after Rabbi Yohanan's criticism.

05.event: Rabbi Zeira, who in Babylonia had believed the Rabbis disagreed with Rabbi's rule, went up to the Land of Israel and found Rabbi Asi teaching otherwise.
05.turn: Rabbi Asi taught in Rabbi Yohanan's name that all agree with the rule, and the dispute concerned a different formula.
05.outcome: His earlier understanding is corrected; nothing further happens.
05.summary: In Babylonia, Rabbi Zeira and his colleagues assumed the Rabbis disputed a ruling about conditions. When he moved to the Land of Israel he found Rabbi Asi teaching, in Rabbi Yohanan's name, that everyone agrees with that ruling and the disagreement is only about saying 'from today and after my death'.
05.missing: Little action beyond hearing a teaching; it is mainly a report of a tradition.

06.event: Judges in Neharde'a and Rav Hana bar Bizna in Pumbedita ordered daughters supported from movable property.
06.turn: Rav Nahman ordered them to reverse their rulings, threatening to seize their houses otherwise.
06.outcome: The threat is issued; whether they complied is not told.
06.summary: Courts in Neharde'a and Pumbedita ruled that a dead man's daughters should be supported from his movable property, and Rav Hana bar Bizna collected the money. Rav Nahman told the judges to reverse their decisions, or he would take their own houses to repay those they had ruled against.
06.missing: Whether the judges reversed their rulings.

07.event: A man told witnesses that if he did not marry his betrothed by the New Moon of Adar, his document would be a bill of divorce.
07.turn: When Adar arrived he claimed he had said Nisan.
07.outcome: The text turns to legal analysis; no ruling or outcome for the couple is given.
07.summary: A man set a condition that his bill of divorce would take effect if he did not marry his fiancee by the New Moon of Adar. When the date came and he had not married her, he claimed he had actually said Nisan. The Gemara then analyzes what legal concern might apply, without telling how the case ended.
07.missing: The ruling or outcome of the case.

08.event: Rabbi Yehoshua went to study with Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri and found him sitting among trees.
08.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua stretched a vine between two trees and asked whether one could sow seeds on the other side.
08.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri answered that it is permitted if the trees are ten cubits apart and forbidden if more.
08.summary: Although he was already an expert in the laws of mixed planting, Rabbi Yehoshua went to learn from Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri. Finding him among the trees, he stretched a vine from one tree to another and asked whether seeds could be sown beyond it. Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri ruled that it is allowed if the trees are up to ten cubits apart, and forbidden if farther.

09.actor: a man in Rabbi Ami's neighborhood
09.event: Rabbi Ami publicly declared a neighbor to be a mamzer.
09.outcome: Rabbi Ami told him that by declaring it he had given him life.
09.summary: A man living near Rabbi Ami was publicly declared by him to be a mamzer, of illegitimate birth. The man went around crying over it. Rabbi Ami told him that he had in fact given him life, since a known mamzer is not struck down from Heaven.

10.event: Rabbi once ruled in a case following Rabbi Elazar's opinion.
10.turn: Afterward he remembered that Rabbi Elazar's view was contested.
10.outcome: He said Rabbi Elazar is worthy to rely on in a pressing situation.
10.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once decided a case according to Rabbi Elazar. Later he recalled that Rabbi Elazar's colleagues disagreed with him. Rather than retract, he said that Rabbi Elazar is a fit authority to rely on in times of need.

11.actor: Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok and his family
11.event: One year the Ninth of Av fell on Shabbat, so the family of Sena'av ben Binyamin postponed the fast to Sunday.
11.outcome: They fasted but did not complete the fast.
11.summary: Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok recalled that his family, descendants of Sena'av ben Binyamin, kept a family festival on the tenth of Av. One year the Ninth of Av fell on Shabbat and the fast was moved to Sunday, their festival day. They fasted part of the day but broke the fast before evening because of their festival.

12.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment from someone else's beer.
12.turn: The owner found him and asked why he had not used the better, sharper sediment, which the brewer took as consent.
12.outcome: Rava ruled that such a remark counts as consent only for teruma, so the brewer had no right to the sediment.
12.summary: A brewer making beer for someone betrothed a woman using some of the beer sediment. The owner caught him and asked why he hadn't used the better sediment instead. The brewer asked Rava whether that showed consent, and Rava said such a remark counts as consent only in the case of teruma, not here.

13.actor: an unnamed questioner and the people of Judea
13.event: Following Rabbi Abba's suggestion, someone asked the people of Judea how two words in the mishna were spelled.
13.turn: They answered that both spellings were in use.
13.outcome: The question was settled as both versions being valid.
13.summary: Rabbi Abba wished someone would ask the people of Judea, known for precise language, whether two mishnaic words were spelled with an alef or an ayin. Someone asked them, and they answered that some taught one spelling and some the other.
13.missing: Hardly any event; it is mainly a reported answer about a textual reading.

14.event: Rabbi Elazar missed the study hall one day and asked Rabbi Asi what had been taught.
14.turn: Rabbi Asi told him Rabbi Yohanan ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
14.outcome: The report is given; the conversation continues as legal discussion.
14.summary: Rabbi Elazar did not attend the study hall one day. Meeting Rabbi Asi, he asked what the Sages had said there, and Rabbi Asi reported Rabbi Yohanan's ruling that the law follows Rabbi Yosei.
14.missing: Little beyond the transmission of a ruling; no real turn or ending.

15.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya
15.event: When Rabbi fell ill, Rabbi Hiyya visited him and found him crying.
15.turn: Rabbi Hiyya asked why he wept, since dying in tears is a bad omen.
15.outcome: Rabbi answered that he was crying for the Torah and mitzvot he would no longer be able to fulfill.
15.summary: When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi fell ill, Rabbi Hiyya came to see him and found him crying. He asked why, reminding him of the tradition that dying while crying is a bad sign, and listing other omens at death. Rabbi replied that he was weeping over the Torah and commandments he would lose the chance to keep.

16.event: Abdan's daughters-in-law rebelled against their husbands, and Rabbi sent two Sages to examine them.
16.turn: When women pointed out their husbands approaching, they retorted, 'Let them be your husbands.'
16.outcome: Rabbi declared there is no greater refusal than this.
16.summary: The daughters-in-law of Abdan rebelled against their husbands, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sent a pair of Sages to look into the matter. Other women said to them, 'Look, your husbands are coming,' and they answered, 'Let them be your husbands.' Rabbi ruled that there could be no clearer act of refusal.

17.actor: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva
17.event: The Sages were sailing from Pelandarsin when their boat set out to sea on Shabbat, beyond the Shabbat limit.
17.turn: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya walked the whole boat while Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva stayed within four cubits.
17.outcome: The two groups simply behaved differently; no further resolution.
17.summary: Four Sages were traveling by ship from Pelandarsin when it sailed out to sea on Shabbat. Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya walked about the whole ship, while Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva, wanting to be strict with themselves, did not move beyond four cubits.
17.missing: A turn or ending beyond the contrast in behavior.

18.event: Rava asked Rav Nahman which tanna rejects retroactive designation even for rabbinic laws, citing a baraita.
18.turn: Rav Nahman fell silent and gave no answer.
18.summary: Rava challenged Rav Nahman to identify the tanna behind a baraita about choosing an eiruv recipient after nightfall. Rav Nahman stayed silent and said nothing.
18.missing: Mostly legal argument; the only event is the unanswered question.

19.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
19.event: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua conducted a halitza ceremony before five judges.
19.outcome: The Gemara explains they did so to publicize the matter.
19.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua performed a halitza ceremony with five judges rather than three. The Gemara explains this was to make the event widely known, not because five were required.
19.missing: A turn or developed narrative; it is a brief report of a practice.

20.event: Doubting a ruling Rav Beruna attributed to Shmuel, Rabbi Elazar went to Shmuel's lodging and asked him directly.
20.turn: Shmuel confirmed it, and Rabbi Elazar objected with Shmuel's own earlier statement.
20.summary: Rav Beruna was teaching a ruling in Shmuel's name about alleyways. Rabbi Elazar doubted it and asked to be shown Shmuel's lodging, went there, and asked Shmuel, who confirmed it. Rabbi Elazar then confronted him with his own principle that eiruv law follows the wording of the mishna, and Shmuel had no answer.
